runs.text: pera diante, ou pera baixo com algum pao, ou

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's definition of tsuku: thrusting forwards or downwards with a stick. The definition remains physically divided across pages.

runs.text: outro inſtrumento, como quem dà com bordão

lines.note: The action uses another implement or a staff; the following row supplies leaning and pointed thrusts as examples. Bordão retains its printed nasal mark.

runs.text: encostandoſe, ou dà destocadas, ou de ponta,

lines.note: Describes leaning on a support or giving thrusts with a point. The missing vowel in OCR encstandoſe is restored from the visible enco-; the printed contractions are retained.
Boo wo tsuku and tsue wo tsuku illustrate planting or using a staff. Latin l introduces the alternative example, and the caron on Bǒ is visible.

runs.text: Dar com algum pao, ou bordão como quem vai

lines.note: The Portuguese begins explaining use of a stick or staff while walking. This is the translation of the preceding Japanese examples, not another headword.
Completes walking while leaning on the staff; Catana wo begins a new example about using a sword as a prop. The small printed space in a elle is retained.
The sword is used in place of a stick or staff to lean on. Catana is a Japanese-derived weapon name embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: de pao pera ſe encoſtar, ou bordão. ¶

lines.note: Completes the support or walking-stick sense, then Co- begins kome, rice, on the next physical row. Its visible terminal hyphen is preserved.
Kome wo tsuku means pounding rice; tsuchi begins the next example about pounding earth. Both examples illustrate the physical striking sense of tsuku.

runs.text: Bater, ou pilar a terra como quẽ

lines.note: Tsuchi wo tsuku is beating or tamping earth. The Portuguese comparison continues below with construction of a rammed-earth wall.

Completes the taipa comparison, then introduces ken wo motte hito wo tsuku, striking someone with a sword. The capital Q's broad tail accounts for the OCR's false gap in Qenuo, as comparison with Qi below confirms.

runs.text: Dar destocadas com eſpada ẽ alguẽ.

lines.note: Completes the sword example with tsuku; the Portuguese specifies sword thrusts at someone. The damaged st group has been read with the neighbouring destocadas example.
Yari wo tsuku means thrusting with a spear, matching dar lançadas. Visible Yariuo replaces the malformed OCR Yurino; Ta- begins tate, shield.
Tate wo tsuku is erecting shields or defensive boards in the Japanese manner. The Portuguese explanation continues on the next row.

runs.text: fixando hũas taboas no chão como repairo.

lines.note: The boards are fixed in the ground as protection. This completes the shield example, retaining the historical Portuguese repairo.
Yama wo tsuku and tsukiaguru refer to building up a mound. The Portuguese verb fazer begins at the physical line end.

runs.text: zer montes às mãos, l, à enxada. ¶

lines.note: Completes fazer and describes making mounds by hand or with a hoe. Tçu- begins the noun tsukiyama; the initial zer is not OCR zes.
Tsukiyama denotes an artificially made hill or mound. The printed gap in qi yama is retained without changing the compound's interpretation.
Tori wo tsuku describes striking over birds with a net. The Portuguese specifies the net and continues with the birds' flight below.
The birds are caught while flying; tsukiami names the net used for this action. The final consonant is m, correcting OCR Tçuqiani.

runs.text: Rede com que dão ſobre algũs paßaros, & os

lines.note: Defines the tsukiami as a net brought down over certain birds to catch them. The whole Portuguese word paßaros is italic, including the OCR's stray roman a.

Completes catching the birds, then begins an example in which an ox or the animal yagiuu, here glossed cabra, strikes a person. The weak letter before ǔ is read as i rather than OCR r; the caron is retained.

runs.text: Dar o boy, ou cabra em alguem com os

lines.note: Completes tsuku; Portuguese dar o boy, ou cabra explains the animal's striking action. The implement, its horns, is specified on the next row.
Completes the goring example with horns, then iki wo tsuku introduces breathing or exhaling. This starts a distinct figurative extension of the same verb.
Respirar completes the preceding breathing gloss. This short continuation belongs to iki wo tsuku, rather than the following verb of attachment.
Tsuki, tsuku, tsuita here means sticking or adhering. Sumi ga te-ni tsuita introduces the example of ink sticking to the hands; the OCR's extra j and Simi are corrected from the print.
Completes the ink example and begins hito no te ni tsuku. The Portuguese first says the ink stuck to the hands; Fi- starts hito on the next row.
Hito no te ni tsuku means being with someone or under that person's control. Its protective or dependent sense is made explicit in the following Portuguese continuation.

runs.text: baixo de ſeu mando, ou proteição. ¶

lines.note: Completes being under another's command or protection; Ten- begins tengu. This remains a continuation of attachment or possession, not the exhaustiveness sense below.
Tengu ga hito ni tsuku is demonic possession, glossed as the devil entering someone. The scan reads diabo rather than OCR doabo.
Tsuki, tsukuru, tsukita means coming to an end or being used up. The visible principal-part ending ita replaces OCR ica and distinguishes this verb from tsuku, to adhere.
Inochi or takara ga tsukuru describes life or possessions running out. The Portuguese translation begins acaba- and continues on the next row.
Completes the ending of life or wealth, then un ga tsu- begins an example about fortune running out. The physical split of the Japanese verb is preserved.
Tsukita completes un ga tsukita: luck or good fortune has ended. Qi begins another example referring to energy or vital force.
Ki or sei ga tsukita describes becoming exhausted or faint. The Portuguese gloss carries on with absence of strength below.
Sem forças completes the description as being without strength. This short row belongs to the exhaustion example and remains separately transcribed.
The noun tsuki denotes exhaustion or ending. Tçu- begins tsukisenu, the negative form in the following example.
Tsukisenu koto denotes something inexhaustible or infinite. The historical negative senu is printed xenu here and is not modernized.
Ca completes Portuguese nunca, explaining something that never ends. The short continuation finishes tsukisenu koto before the next headword.
Tsukiage describes raising a wall or mound by working earth. The Portuguese co- continues as como on the following line.

runs.text: mo taipa, ou monte de terra, &c. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes the comparison with a rammed-earth wall or earthen mound. Item introduces the separate completive sense on the next row.

runs.text: Acabar de fazer, ou aleuantar taipa, &c.

lines.note: The second sense is finishing the construction or raising of a rammed-earth wall. The compound's completive interpretation agrees with acabar de fazer.
Tsukiai denotes the interval between one month and the next. Vt introduces an example whose Japanese text begins on the following row.
Tsukiai ni mairoozu means intending to go at the turn of the month. No paragraph sign precedes the printed example; the OCR's extra sign is removed.
Specifies either the end of the present month or the start of the next. This completes the temporal tsukiai example.
A separate tsukiai entry concerns commerce and contact among different regions or peoples. The word partes is divided with a visible terminal hyphen.
Tsukiai no tokoro is a place of such commerce; Portuguese Lu continues as gar at the head of column 2. The restored i in Tçuqiaino and capital L are visible; no hyphen is supplied after Lu.

runs.text: gar onde ha este commercio como eſcala, &c.

lines.note: Gar completes Lu from column 1: a place where commerce occurs, such as a trading stop or port. The visible double m corrects OCR conmercio.
The reciprocal verb tsukiau describes two or more parties exchanging spear thrusts. Both long-o marks are carons; the Portuguese plural continuation follows below.

runs.text: is, ou darenſe de adagadas, ou estocadas.

lines.note: Completes mais and adds dagger blows or thrusts as alternatives. The printed n in darenſe is retained rather than regularized to modern Portuguese.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Chegar a hum lugar de diuerſas par-

lines.note: Item adds a sense of arriving at one place from different directions or regions. The divided Portuguese partes continues onto the following row.

runs.text: tes. ¶ Item, Encontrarenſe com os cornos

lines.note: Completes the converging-arrival sense, then introduces animals meeting or striking each other with their horns. Both clauses belong to tsukiau.
Specifies oxen and deer as the horned animals. This short continuation finishes the reciprocal striking entry before tsukikakaru.
Tsukikakari, tsukikakaru, tsukikakatta means encountering or colliding with someone. The Portuguese explanation continues below with a road encounter.

runs.text: dar de encõtro com alguem como no caminho,

lines.note: Describes bumping into someone, for example on a road. The nasal abbreviation in encõtro is retained without expansion.

runs.text: &c. Itẽ, Dar ſobre alguẽ cõ lãça, ou eſtocadas.

lines.note: Adds an aggressive sense: attacking someone with a spear or thrusts. The tildes in alguẽ, cõ and lãça remain literal abbreviations.
Tsukikage denotes the moon's shadow or likeness. The initial is a damaged capital T, replacing the OCR long-s, and the separate cague is retained.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Claridade, ou rayo da lũa. Vt,

lines.note: Adds moonlight or a moonbeam as another sense. Vt introduces the Japanese example of moonlight entering a place.
Tsukikage ga sasu means that moonlight shines or comes in. The Portuguese begins entering the moon's light, with its destination supplied below.
Completes the gloss as moonlight entering some place. Algũa retains the mark on u visible in this occurrence.
Tsukikazashi, tsukikazasu, tsukikazaita refers to holding something up as a shield or protection. The faint g in algũa is restored from the scan.

runs.text: couſa como com rodela, &c. ou pondoa por

lines.note: A shield or similar object provides the protection, or is placed to cover another thing. The final a in pondoa refers back to the protective object, correcting OCR pondos.
Completes emparo, protection, and begins a cited example with ichimai hagi. The apparent gap inside emparo is due to the weakly printed r rather than a separate word.
Completes ichimai hagi no wataridate and places the light shields at the horses' heads. The example continues with tsuki-kazaite below; the initial t in tçuqi is visible.
Cazaite is the historical inflected form of kazasu, followed by the citation label Yax. The Portuguese translation begins placing the shields at the horses' heads.

runs.text: dos caualos hũas rodelas leues de hũa ſoò taboa.

lines.note: Completes the translation: light shields made of a single board are held at the horses' heads. The printed grave in ſoò is retained.
Tsukikomi, tsukikomu, tsukikonda means thrusting in a spear or similar implement. The principal part uses the visibly circumflexed ôda abbreviation.

Adaga completes the spear-or-dagger example, then miso wo tsukikomu introduces packing miso firmly into a container. The damaged d is restored from its tall stem and bowl remnants; Cal- continues as calcar below.

runs.text: car bem o Miſo dentro dalgum vaſo, &c.

lines.note: Car completes calcar: pressing miso firmly inside a vessel. Miſo occurs within the Portuguese explanation and is retained in its printed italic type.
Tsukikoroshi, tsukikorosu, tsukikoroita means killing with spear thrusts, dagger blows, or stabs. The divided adagadas continues below; oita is retained as the historical principal part.

runs.text: gadas, ou eſtocadas. ¶ Itẽ, Matar cõ os cornos.

lines.note: Completes the stabbing gloss and adds killing with horns. This closes the killing-by-thrusting entry rather than beginning another headword.
Tsukikusa is identified only as an herb bearing this name. The scan supports chamada, correcting OCR chamida without assigning a modern botanical species.
Tsukikuzushi, tsukikuzusu, tsukikuzuita means knocking down or demolishing. The headword has c, not OCR r, after qi; the Portuguese reads Deſtruir.
Explains demolition by blows or collisions. Item then begins an additional description of destructive spear thrusts on the following row.
Gives destroying with spear thrusts as the added sense. This continuation remains under tsukikuzusu, distinct from the next earthwork term.
Tsukidashi, tsukidasu, tsukidaita concerns extending an earthen embankment or platform. The scan supports ſu, aita and terripleno, repairing the malformed OCR.

Completes extending the ground by making an earthwork. The omitted far-right parenthesis and &c. are restored in their physical position; they may complete the following porto example and are not moved into its row.

runs.text: Lugar onde ſe chega, como porto,

lines.note: Tsukidokoro denotes a place of arrival, such as a port. The comma after porto remains, with the possibly associated &c. preserved above at the far right.
Tsukihanashi, tsukihanasu, tsukihanaita means releasing or pushing something away. Its physical manner is explained by the following hand-action example.

runs.text: de ſi, como quem da com a mão, &c.

lines.note: Completes pushing something away from oneself, as with a blow of the hand. The unaccented da is retained as printed.

runs.text: Sino que ſe tange, ou em que dão

lines.note: Tsukigane is a bell sounded by striking it. The Portuguese description continues below with the striking implement.
Specifies striking the bell with a wooden stick. This completes the bell definition, distinct from the carpenter's tool below.
Tsukiganna is glossed cepilho, a carpenter's plane. The doubled n in the Japanese form and the Portuguese historical spelling are preserved.

runs.text: Os primeiros dias da lũa atè os

lines.note: Tsukigashira denotes the first days of a lunar month. Primeiros dias replaces the OCR's malformed grimeiros diux and leads into the numerical limit below.
Specifies the first four or five days of the month. This short continuation completes the temporal noun tsukigashira.
Tsukigoto or tsukigotoni is equated with maiguat, every month. The final t in Maiguat is a historical checked syllable and is retained without expansion.
Cada lũa, ou cada mes gives the monthly meaning directly. The Japanese synonym above is not part of Portuguese prose for typeface marking.
Tsukige names a white or pale horse colour in this gloss. Item introduces the horse described by this colour, whose name continues across the row break.
Completes tsukige and tsukige no uma: a horse of the stated colour. The printed deſte cor is retained despite the grammatical gender mismatch.

Tsukiire describes thrusting something inside by striking or touching it. Both i types are visible in the enlarged headword; the supplied NINJAL index independently identifies Tçuqiire, without determining the local typography.
Completes causing something to enter by making contact with it. The Portuguese metela retains the unhyphenated pronoun attachment.

runs.text: O eſperar pella lũa quando ſae q̃

lines.note: Tsukimachi means waiting for the moon's rising. The faint rounded vowel in pella is e, not OCR i; the description continues with the religious observance below.

runs.text: he hũa ceremonia dos gẽtios. Vt,

lines.note: Explains the moon-waiting as a ceremony of non-Christians, then begins tsukimachi wo suru. The compressed gẽtios is retained with its visible tilde and faint e rather than expanded to gentios.
Chi completes tsukimachi; wo suru means performing the moon-waiting observance. This is the final running-text row; the repeated Tçuqi- below is a catchword.
Repeats the beginning of Tçuqimairi on f490. The visible terminal hyphen is retained; this is page furniture, not an additional body entry.
